title: Automatic Certificate Management Environment (ACME)
organization: Cisco / EFF / Let's Encrypt / University of Michigan

hero.subtitle: The protocol behind Let's Encrypt that automated certificate issuance and renewal, bringing free HTTPS to the entire web.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ACME (Automatic Certificate Management Environment) automates the process of verification and issuance of X.509 certificates. It was designed for Let's Encrypt but is used by many CAs.

Before ACME, getting an SSL certificate required manual steps, payment, and waiting. ACME made free, automated certificates possible, helping make HTTPS the norm on the web.
sections.plainLanguage: ACME (Automatic Certificate Management Environment) automates checking domain ownership and issuing X.509 certificates, the files that let browsers trust a website. It was designed for Let's Encrypt but many certificate authorities (CAs) now use it. Before ACME, getting a certificate involved manual steps, payment and waiting.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
ACME is a JSON-based protocol over HTTPS. All POST requests are signed with the account's private key using JWS (JSON Web Signature).

Account CreationClient registers a public key with the CA server
OrderClient requests a certificate for one or more domain names
AuthorizationCA presents challenges to prove domain control
FinalizeClient submits CSR, CA issues the certificate
sections.plainLanguage: ACME is a JSON-based protocol that runs over HTTPS. Every POST request is signed with the account's private key using JWS (JSON Web Signature). The steps are: the client registers an account key, orders a certificate for one or more domain names, proves control of each domain, and submits a certificate signing request (CSR) so the CA can issue the certificate.

sections.title: Challenge Types
sections.content:
ACME supports multiple challenge types to prove domain control:

Challenge
Mechanism
HTTP-01
Place a file at /.well-known/acme-challenge/ on port 80
DNS-01
Create a TXT record _acme-challenge.domain
TLS-ALPN-01
Present a self-signed cert during TLS on port 443 (defined separately in RFC 8737, not in RFC 8555)

In practice, wildcard certificates (*.example.com) are validated with DNS-01; Let's Encrypt requires it.
sections.plainLanguage: To prove it controls a domain, the client completes a challenge. With HTTP-01 it places a file under /.well-known/acme-challenge/ on port 80. With DNS-01 it creates a TXT record named _acme-challenge under the domain. TLS-ALPN-01 is defined separately in RFC 8737. Let's Encrypt requires DNS-01 for wildcard certificates.

sections.title: Automated Renewal
sections.content:
The RFC does not set a certificate lifetime, but Let's Encrypt has issued 90-day certificates, which encourages automation. Clients like Certbot, acme.sh, and Caddy handle automatic renewal.

Certbot
The most popular ACME client, developed by EFF. Supports Apache, Nginx, and standalone modes.
Short-Lived Certs
Short validity reduces exposure if a key is compromised and encourages automation.
Rate Limits
Let's Encrypt enforces rate limits on issuance to prevent abuse.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not set a certificate lifetime. Let's Encrypt has issued 90-day certificates, which makes automatic renewal necessary, and clients such as Certbot, acme.sh and Caddy do it. Short lifetimes limit the damage if a key is compromised. Let's Encrypt also applies rate limits on issuance to prevent abuse.

subtitle: The protocol behind Let's Encrypt that automated certificate issuance and renewal, bringing free HTTPS to the entire web.
summary: ACME lets software ask a certificate authority for an X.509 certificate and prove control of a domain, with no human involved. Requests are JSON messages sent over HTTPS and signed with an account key. It is the protocol behind Let's Encrypt and is now used by many certificate authorities.

plainLanguage.summary: ACME lets software ask a certificate authority for an X.509 certificate and prove control of a domain with no human involved. Requests are JSON messages sent over HTTPS and signed with an account key. It is the protocol behind Let's Encrypt and is now used by many certificate authorities.

tldr.problem: Getting and renewing a TLS certificate meant manual forms, emails and waiting.
tldr.mechanism: A client registers an account key, places an order, answers a challenge that proves domain control, then submits a CSR to finalize.
tldr.outcome: Certificates can be issued and renewed automatically, which made free, widespread HTTPS practical.

questions: how does let's encrypt verify domain ownership
what is the difference between http-01 and dns-01
how do wildcard certificates work with acme
how does certbot renew certificates automatically
today: ACME clients such as Certbot, acme.sh and Caddy renew certificates automatically, and Let's Encrypt and other certificate authorities speak the protocol. Later extensions add more challenge types such as TLS-ALPN-01 (RFC 8737) and certificates for IP addresses. Shorter certificate lifetimes across the web depend on ACME-style automation.

messages.note: Each authorization lists challenges the client can choose from.

messages.note: The client has provisioned the http-01 file or dns-01 TXT record and tells the server to validate.

messages.label: Authorization valid
messages.note: The server validated the challenge. The order becomes ready.

messages.note: Submits a PKCS#10 certificate signing request.

messages.note: Order is valid; the client downloads the certificate chain.
